desc:
Every cell of the rectangular grid holds a non-negative toll. A route starts in the top-left cell, ends in the bottom-right cell and moves only one step right or one step down at a time. Its cost is the sum of the tolls of all cells on it, including the first and the last one.

Several routes may share the smallest possible cost. Return how many different routes have exactly that smallest cost, modulo 1,000,000,007. Two routes are different if they visit different sequences of cells.
hints: Computing only the cheapest cost is the standard minimum path sum. You need to know in how many ways that cost is reached, so store two numbers per cell.
For each cell keep a pair: the cheapest cost cost to reach it and the number ways of reaching it at exactly that cost.

Compare the pairs of the cell above and the cell to the left. The smaller cost wins and its ways is inherited; on a tie, add both ways. Then add the cell's own toll to the cost. Reduce ways modulo 1,000,000,007 as you go.
editorial: A cheapest route to a cell is a cheapest route to one of its two predecessors followed by the cell itself: if the prefix was not optimal for the predecessor, a better prefix would give a cheaper route to the cell. So the cheapest cost satisfies cost[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(cost[r-1][c], cost[r][c-1]), and the cheapest routes to the cell are exactly the cheapest routes to those predecessors whose cost equals that minimum.

Therefore ways[r][c] is the sum of ways over the predecessors that attain the minimum: one of them when their costs differ, both when they tie. Tolls of 0 are allowed and cause many ties, which is why the count can grow quickly and is reported modulo 1,000,000,007. Note that costs themselves must be compared exactly, only the counts are reduced. Time O(m · n), space O(n) with a rolling row.
